subtopics.title: Social, cultural, political, economic and historical contexts

outcomes.text: Explain how media products differ in institutional background and use of media language, and can reflect or construct social, cultural and political attitudes.
Explain how media products reflect historical issues and events.
Explain how media products can help drive social, cultural and political change through viewpoints, messages and values.
Explain how contexts influence media products through intertextual references.
Explain how media products reflect economic contexts through production, finance and technological opportunities and constraints.
Explain how the modes (images, sound, speech, writing) and language of different media forms communicate multiple meanings.
Explain how combinations of media language elements influence meaning.
Explain how developing technologies affect media language.
Identify the codes and conventions of forms and products, including how media language develops as genre.
Explain that genre is dynamic and historically relative.
Explain how meanings are established through intertextuality, and its varied uses.
Explain how audiences respond to and interpret media language.
Explain how genre conventions are socially and historically relative, and can be hybrid.
Evaluate the significance of challenging or subverting genre conventions.
Explain how media language incorporates viewpoints and ideologies.
Apply semiotics, including Barthes.
Apply narratology, including Todorov.
Apply genre theory, including Neale.
Apply structuralism, including Lévi-Strauss.
Apply postmodernism, including Baudrillard.

subtopics.title: How the media represent the world

outcomes.text: Explain how events, issues, individuals and social groups are represented through selection and combination.
Explain how re-presentation constructs versions of reality.
Explain why producers make particular choices about representation.
Explain the effect of social and cultural context on representations.
Explain how and why stereotypes can be used positively and negatively.
Explain how social groups may be under-represented or misrepresented nationally and globally.
Explain how representations convey values, attitudes and beliefs, and how these are reinforced across media.
Explain how audiences respond to and interpret representations.
Explain how representations make claims about realism.
Explain the impact of industry contexts on representation choices.
Explain the effect of historical context on representations.
Explain how representations invoke discourses and ideologies and position audiences.
Explain how audience responses to representations reflect social, cultural and historical circumstances.
Apply theories of representation, including Hall.
Apply theories of identity, including Gauntlett.
Apply feminist theories, including bell hooks and Van Zoonen.
Apply theories of gender performativity, including Butler.
Apply theories of ethnicity and postcolonial theory, including Gilroy.
Explain processes of production, distribution and circulation by organisations, groups and individuals in a global context.
Explain the specialised and institutionalised nature of media production, distribution and circulation.
Explain the relationship between recent technological change and production, distribution and circulation.
Explain how processes of production, distribution and circulation shape media products.
Explain the impact of digitally convergent media platforms, including on individual producers.
Explain the effect of individual producers on media industries.
Explain patterns of ownership and control: conglomerates, vertical integration and diversification.
Explain the significance of economic factors, including commercial and not-for-profit public funding.
Explain how organisations maintain audiences nationally and globally, including through marketing.
Explain the regulatory framework of UK media.
Explain the impact of digital technologies on regulation, including individual producers.
Explain the role of regulation in global production, distribution and circulation.
Apply theories of power and media industries, including Curran and Seaton.
Apply theories of regulation, including Livingstone and Lunt.
Apply theories of cultural industries, including Hesmondhalgh.
Explain how audiences are grouped and categorised by age, gender, social class, lifestyle and taste.
Explain how producers target, attract, reach, address and potentially construct audiences.
Explain how industries target audiences through content, appeal, marketing, distribution and circulation.
Explain the interrelationship between media technologies and patterns of consumption and response.
Explain how specialised audiences are reached nationally and globally through different technologies.
Explain how organisations meet the needs of mass and specialised audiences.
Explain how audiences interpret the same media in different ways.
Explain how audiences interact with the media and can be actively involved in production.
Explain how audiences use media differently, reflecting demographics, identity and cultural capital.
Explain the role of specialised audiences, including niche and fan audiences.
Explain how different interpretations reflect social, cultural and historical circumstances.
Apply media effects theory, including Bandura.
Apply cultivation theory, including Gerbner.
Apply reception theory, including Hall.
Apply theories of fandom, including Jenkins.
Apply theories of the 'end of audience', including Shirky.

topics.title: Section A: News and online media

outcomes.text: Study a Daily Mail and a Guardian edition for how technological change affects newspaper production, distribution and circulation.
Explain the impact of digital convergence on newspapers' offline and online offerings.
Explain ownership and economic factors, including paywalls, subscriptions and online monetisation.
Explain how content and appeal target and address audiences, and how audiences use news differently.
Explain the regulatory framework of the newspaper industry and the impact of online and social media on it.
Analyse how events, issues, individuals and social groups are represented in Daily Mail and Guardian front covers through selection and combination.
Explain how industry contexts such as ownership shape representation choices.
Analyse how representations make claims about realism and use stereotypes.
Analyse how news media language carries viewpoints and ideologies and positions audiences.
Analyse media language on front covers: layout, typography, images and address.
Study Mail Online and Guardian websites, and their Facebook, X and Instagram feeds, for industries and audiences.
Compare articles and feeds with the front covers for language and representation.
Explain how multiple meanings are communicated across platforms and how technology affects media language.
Explain how social and participatory media engage audiences in the news.

topics.title: Section B: Media language and representation

outcomes.text: Study the Dove, River Island and Shelter adverts for the codes and conventions of each category of advert.
Analyse how advertising media language constructs representations.
Explain the social and cultural contexts that shape the adverts' representations.
Study two Big Issue front covers as an alternative to mainstream magazines.
Analyse how magazine media language constructs alternative representations for a niche audience.
Explain the social, cultural and political contexts that shape the representations.
Study one music video from List A and one from List B.
Compare media language and representations between the two videos.
Analyse camera, lighting, setting, costume, editing and sound in music videos.
Explain the social, cultural and historical contexts shaping representations.

topics.title: Section A: Media industries and audiences

outcomes.text: Study Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937) and Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings (2021) in relation to media industries only.
Explain how film production, distribution and circulation changed between 1937 and today.
Explain ownership patterns and Disney as a global conglomerate.
Explain the significance of technological change, regulation and economic factors in the film industry.
Study one complete episode of The BBC Radio One Breakfast Show for industries and audiences.
Explain public service broadcasting and the ethos to inform, educate and entertain.
Explain the distinctiveness of the programme compared with commercial radio and the audiences targeted.
Explain how funding influences content, production, marketing and distribution.
Explain how technology distributes the show across platforms beyond traditional radio.
Study Animal Crossing: New Horizons (2020) for industries and audiences.
Explain ownership in a global context through Nintendo.
Explain how producers have engaged with and constructed their audience.
Explain the influence of technology on production and distribution.

topics.title: Section B: Long form television drama

outcomes.text: Compare one US and one European non-English long form television drama episode as an in-depth study.
Apply all four areas of the theoretical framework and relevant contexts to the set episodes.
Explain the influence of technological change and digital platforms on production, marketing and distribution in a global context.
Explain how audiences consume and interpret long form drama differently, including demographic and technological factors.
Explain how media language subverts genre conventions, with genre hybridity, intertextuality, multiple narrative strands and fandom.
Analyse media-form-specific language: camera, lighting, setting, costume, editing and sound.
Explain how representations carry values and ideologies and position audiences, and reflect social and cultural circumstances.
Explain how economic context shapes the budgets of contemporary US drama.
